recipes.evidence: The two machine-readable halves of external-provider oversight. First, the compliance artifact catalogue AWS publishes about itself — every report, the audit period each one covers, and the two-step token exchange that downloads the document an assessor actually reads. Second, the inventory of external services this account depends on: the VPC endpoints it consumes, which name the provider on the far side of a connection (an interface endpoint IS PrivateLink; the service is not listed separately because what these commands read is a VPC endpoint), and the SAML and OpenID Connect providers it trusts to authenticate people into it.
recipes.expected_output: From artifact-reports, reports[] — a page of the report resources this account can see, each carrying id (pattern report- plus sixteen characters), name, description, series, category, companyName, productName, version (a whole number starting at 1), periodStart and periodEnd as timestamps bounding the audit window the document covers, state of PUBLISHED or UNPUBLISHED, uploadState of PROCESSING, COMPLETE, FAILED or FAULT, acceptanceType of PASSTHROUGH or EXPLICIT, and statusMessage. The page is capped at three hundred entries and continues through nextToken. companyName and productName are members of the row shape rather than guaranteed fields, and their presence is the clue that the catalogue is not only AWS's own documents — read what came back rather than assuming the publisher. From artifact-report-metadata, reportDetails — one report's full record, with the ReportSummary fields plus createdAt, lastModifiedAt, deletedAt, termArn and sequenceNumber; its periodEnd is the audit window of the report YOU named, which is the field a freshness claim has to be made against. From artifact-report-term, documentPresignedUrl — the terms document itself — and termToken, a single-use token representing this request event. From artifact-report, documentPresignedUrl: a presigned S3 URL, no longer than 10,240 characters, that resolves to the report content; the call requires reportId and termToken and will not return a document without the token the term call just issued. From third-party-endpoints, VpcEndpoints[] with VpcEndpointId, VpcEndpointType of Interface, Gateway, GatewayLoadBalancer, Resource or ServiceNetwork, VpcId, ServiceName, OwnerId, CreationTimestamp, PolicyDocument, Tags, ServiceNetworkArn and ResourceConfigurationArn, and a State among PendingAcceptance, Pending, Available, Deleting, Deleted, Rejected, Failed, Expired and Partial — the ServiceName of an endpoint that does not begin com.amazonaws. is a service somebody else operates, and the name is the provider. From saml-providers, SAMLProviderList[] with Arn, CreateDate and an OPTIONAL ValidUntil, the expiry of the federation metadata that trust rests on. From oidc-providers, OpenIDConnectProviderList[] with Arn and nothing else — the ARN's own suffix is the provider's hostname, and it is the only identifying field the list call returns.
recipes.govcloud: AWS Artifact runs in AWS GovCloud (US) and its own GovCloud page states, in full, that "There are no differences for this service" — the catalogue, the term exchange and the download behave as they do commercially. Amazon VPC and IAM are available in both AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and every ARN in this output uses partition arn:aws-us-gov. One VPC difference touches this recipe's own output directly: not all VPC endpoints in the partition support endpoint policies, so PolicyDocument may be absent on an endpoint where the commercial Regions would carry one, and its absence is an unsupported endpoint type rather than a removed control — say which it was. Three IAM differences bear on what this evidence can mean, and the third is a fact about external providers rather than about the API. There is one IAM control plane for all GovCloud Regions and it sits in AWS GovCloud (US-West), so the provider lists here are answered from that Region regardless of where you call. A SAML relying party is configured against https://signin.amazonaws-us-gov.com/static/saml-metadata.xml with SAML audience urn:amazon:webservices:govcloud, and the ACS URL is https://signin.amazonaws-us-gov.com/saml, so federation metadata copied from a commercial tenant is wrong in the partition rather than merely different. And you cannot create a role to delegate access between an AWS GovCloud (US) account and a standard AWS account: a provider operating in the commercial partition cannot be handed a role in this account at all, so an external integration that exists commercially as a cross-account role has to take some other shape here, and its absence from these lists is not evidence that the dependency is absent. Finally, AWS documents that IAM metadata is not permitted to contain export-controlled data — role names, policy names and the free-text fields around them included — which constrains what a provider's name may say in a tag.
recipes.notes:
SA-09 has three limbs and this output serves parts of two of them, which is the whole reason for the rating.

The limb it serves best is (c), monitoring a provider's control compliance on an ongoing basis. AWS Artifact is a provider publishing its own audit evidence on a machine-readable channel: list-reports is a catalogue of report resources, get-report-metadata returns one report's record including the audit window it covers, and the term-then-get pair returns the document an assessor asks for. The reader's obligation is to check that the artifact their package leans on still covers a current period — which is a field, not a meeting.

The limb it partly serves is (a), requiring that providers comply with your security and privacy requirements. Requiring is a contract and no command reads one. What these commands produce is the LIST the contract set has to be reconciled against: which external services this account actually consumes and which external identity providers it actually trusts. Most providers cannot produce that list on demand, and a reconciliation against an inventory that was assembled by hand proves nothing about the inventory.

Limb (b) — documented oversight roles and responsibilities — is not addressed here at all and should not be read as covered.

What is NOT in this catalogue is the thing a FedRAMP reader will look for first, and the recipe would be misleading if it did not say so. AWS's own FedRAMP certification package is not an Artifact download: AWS directs customers to obtain it from the FedRAMP PMO by completing a Package Access Request Form. What Artifact carries under that name is the FedRAMP Partner Package, which is guidance for building on AWS rather than AWS's audit report. Treat the catalogue as the channel for the documents that ARE published on it — ISO certifications, PCI and SOC reports among them — and do not write an assessment sentence claiming the FedRAMP package came from an API call.

The catalogue is also not reader-specific, and that is the easiest thing to over-read. Every account with permission sees the same report resources, so a clause over reports[] is a statement about publishing rather than about this estate. The reader-specific facts are which report they named, which terms they accepted, and whether the document their package cites has aged out — which is why the freshness clause below reads get-report-metadata for a single <REPORT_ID> and not the catalogue. A FAIL there means the document YOU cite covers a period that ended more than fifteen months ago; it is a gap in your evidence, never a defect in the provider's.

The download is two calls, and the token between them is the mechanic. get-term-for-report returns the terms document and a termToken representing that request event; get-report will not hand back a presigned URL without it. A collection script that calls get-report alone gets a validation error, and an assessment that cites a report id without ever having run the pair has cited a catalogue entry rather than a document.

The vacuity to state plainly, and it runs the other way here than usual. An account whose caller lacks Artifact permissions gets AccessDeniedException, not an empty list, so an empty reports[] is anomalous rather than innocent — but the clause that separates the two is still the population clause, and it is the first one below. The endpoint and provider lists have the ordinary version of the trap: describe-vpc-endpoints is Regional and returns a history, with Deleted, Rejected and Expired endpoints still in the response, so a count over the raw list counts dependencies that no longer exist; and both IAM provider lists are empty on an account that federates through IAM Identity Center instead of through an account-level provider, which means an empty list says there is no federation OF THIS KIND and never that there is no external identity provider.

No clause here filters endpoints by ServiceName, and the reason is worth recording rather than leaving as a gap. Deciding that a service name belongs to an external provider rather than to your own organization is a comparison against your own supplier list, and an assertion in this grammar compares a field to a constant — the same limitation the internal-connection recipe records about OwnerId. There is a second reason: AWS's own reference does not say whether ServiceName is populated on the newer Resource and ServiceNetwork endpoint types, and a filter that reads a key which may be absent is the shape that raises on exactly the rows it exists to catch. The endpoints are collected as inventory, and the inventory is what the agreement set is reconciled against.

The SAML clause is an operational signal and not a compliance one, and it is spelled in a way that needs saying out loud twice. First, max_age_days 0 reads "not older than zero days", which is true only of a timestamp at or after now — it is this grammar's spelling for "has not yet expired". Second, ValidUntil is an OPTIONAL member: a provider entry that carries no expiry at all is narrowed OUT of the clause by its `where`, deliberately and visibly, because a missing expiry is not an expired one and a projection that silently dropped those rows would be the banned form wearing a plausible face. The providers outside the clause are the ones to read by hand.

KSI-SCR-MIT is claimed for identify-and-review only. Nothing here mitigates a supply-chain risk; it enumerates the suppliers and reads what one of them publishes. KSI-SCR-MON is deliberately NOT claimed: that indicator is about third-party software resources being monitored for upstream vulnerabilities, and no command here reads a vulnerability. The acquisition recipe earns that one.

assertions.description: The provider's compliance channel is reachable and holds at least one fully uploaded report. It is a channel clause and not a precondition for the freshness clause below, which reads its own output and returns UNPROVEN when that output is missing: this one separates a caller whose Artifact permissions were revoked from a catalogue that genuinely returned nothing. The pipe is load-bearing — without it [0] indexes each matched object rather than the filtered list.

The report this assessment names covers an audit period that ended within the last fifteen months — an annual cycle plus a quarter of publication lag. Fifteen months is authored, not AWS's number. The clause reads get-report-metadata for a single report id rather than the catalogue on purpose: a clause over reports[] computes a fact about the provider's publishing schedule, which no reader can act on, while this one says whether the document YOU cite has aged out, which is the reader's own obligation.

The report you cite actually downloaded. get-report returns a presigned URL only when the term token from get-term-for-report is passed with it, so this clause proves the pair was run and the document exists, rather than proving that a catalogue entry with that id does.

No external identity provider whose entry records a metadata expiry has passed it. max_age_days 0 means "not older than zero days", which is only true of a timestamp at or after now — the spelling this grammar has for a deadline that has not passed. ValidUntil is an optional member, so the `where` narrows the population to the providers that have one: a provider with no recorded expiry is stated as outside the clause rather than dropped by a projection, which is the difference between a narrowing and the banned form. An account with no account-level SAML provider returns UNPROVEN, and that is correct — the absence of this kind of federation is not evidence about external providers generally.

scope.note: describe-vpc-endpoints is a Regional call and returns the endpoints of the Region it ran in, so the dependency inventory is one Region's unless the collection is repeated across the enabled set; the IAM provider lists are global and answered once. The Artifact calls have no Region dimension at all — the catalogue is the same everywhere — so nothing about them is narrowed by this scope. `single` is the honest reading of the weakest command in the set, which is why this recipe could not be `full` even if the contract half were machine-readable.

recipes.evidence: The enumerated set of paths into this account that a request can take without presenting an identity: every resource whose policy IAM Access Analyzer reports as allowing public access, the four account-level switches that decide whether an S3 bucket can be made public at all, the Cognito identity pools that issue AWS credentials to guests, and the API Gateway v2 routes whose authorization type is NONE — plus the two Config readings that say whether the rule producing that last answer has ever actually run.
recipes.expected_output: From analyzers, analyzers[] with arn, name, type, createdAt, lastResourceAnalyzed and lastResourceAnalyzedAt, tags, an optional statusReason carrying a code, and a status among ACTIVE, CREATING, DISABLED and FAILED. The call is run unfiltered and the type is read from each row: ACCOUNT, ORGANIZATION, ACCOUNT_UNUSED_ACCESS, ORGANIZATION_UNUSED_ACCESS, ACCOUNT_INTERNAL_ACCESS and ORGANIZATION_INTERNAL_ACCESS. The type is the analyzer's ZONE OF TRUST, not a different product: ACCOUNT and ORGANIZATION are both external-access analyzers and either one answers the public-access question, which is why the clauses below name both and why passing --type ACCOUNT would report an empty list on an estate whose analyzer is organization-scoped. From public-access-findings, findings[] with id, principal as a map, action[], resource, resourceType, resourceOwnerAccount, condition, createdAt, analyzedAt, updatedAt, sources[] of POLICY, BUCKET_ACL, S3_ACCESS_POINT or S3_ACCESS_POINT_ACCOUNT, resourceControlPolicyRestriction, an optional error, a status among ACTIVE, ARCHIVED and RESOLVED, and isPublic — the boolean that says the finding reports a policy allowing PUBLIC access rather than merely external access. isPublic is a filter key on list-findings and is supported on external-access analyzers only — both zones of trust, neither the unused- nor the internal-access families; the filter map takes string operands, which is why the boolean is written "true". From account-public-access-block, PublicAccessBlockConfiguration with BlockPublicAcls, IgnorePublicAcls, BlockPublicPolicy and RestrictPublicBuckets, all booleans. From identity-pools, IdentityPools[] with IdentityPoolId in REGION:GUID form and IdentityPoolName, paginated at sixty per page. From identity-pool, IdentityPoolId, IdentityPoolName, AllowUnauthenticatedIdentities, AllowClassicFlow, SupportedLoginProviders, CognitoIdentityProviders, SamlProviderARNs and IdentityPoolTags — AllowUnauthenticatedIdentities true means the pool hands AWS credentials to callers who presented no identity at all. From api-gwv2-authorization-type-configured, EvaluationResults[] — the routes the managed rule found NON_COMPLIANT, which for API_GWV2_AUTHORIZATION_TYPE_CONFIGURED means an AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Route whose authorization type is NONE. From its evaluation-status sibling, ConfigRulesEvaluationStatus[] with FirstEvaluationStarted, LastSuccessfulEvaluationTime and the failure fields beside them. From configuration-recorder-status, ConfigurationRecordersStatus[] with recording and lastStatus.
recipes.govcloud: Four of the five services here are available in both AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the fifth answer is a hole a reader needs to know about before they plan around it. IAM and IAM Access Analyzer run in both Regions; Access Analyzer POLICY GENERATION is documented as unavailable in the partition, which does not touch these commands, and every ARN — analyzer, resource, finding — uses partition arn:aws-us-gov. Amazon S3 and the account-level public access block run in both Regions; use a FIPS 140-3 endpoint (https://s3-fips.us-gov-west-1.amazonaws.com or https://s3-fips.us-gov-east-1.amazonaws.com) if you have that requirement, write S3 policies with the GovCloud ARN identifier, and note that MFA delete is not available there at all. Amazon Cognito runs in both Regions over FIPS endpoints only (cognito-idp-fips.us-gov-west-1.amazonaws.com and cognito-idp-fips.us-gov-east-1.amazonaws.com), custom user pool domains and Cognito Sync are unavailable, the role a pool assumes must trust the service principal cognito-identity-us-gov.amazonaws.com in US-West or cognito-identity.us-gov-east-1.amazonaws.com in US-East, and in US-East a role name plus session name longer than twenty-four characters can break AssumeRole outright. The hole is AWS Config: API_GWV2_AUTHORIZATION_TYPE_CONFIGURED is excluded from BOTH AWS GovCloud (US-East) and AWS GovCloud (US-West), so the one anonymous surface in this recipe that Access Analyzer cannot see has no managed rule behind it in the partition. A GovCloud reader collects the other seven outputs and reads API Gateway route authorization out of apigatewayv2 get-routes by hand, or writes a custom rule; what they must not do is let the missing rule's silence read as a clean result.
recipes.notes:
AC-14 asks two things: identify the user actions that can be performed on the system without identification or authentication, and document the rationale for them in the security plan. The second is a document. The first is an enumeration, and the enumeration is exactly what these commands are — which is why this is the rare control whose limb (a) is genuinely machine-readable and whose rating still cannot be full.

It cannot be full because the enumeration is bounded by what AWS can see, and the boundary is stateable. IAM Access Analyzer analyzes RESOURCE-BASED POLICIES on a supported set of resource types — S3 buckets and directory buckets, IAM roles, KMS keys, Lambda functions and layers, SQS queues, Secrets Manager secrets, SNS topics, EBS volume snapshots, RDS DB and DB cluster snapshots, ECR repositories, EFS file systems, DynamoDB tables and streams — and nothing else. An application your team wrote that serves an anonymous page from a container behind a load balancer is an unauthenticated user action, it is squarely what AC-14 is about, and no call in this recipe returns it. The honest reading of a clean result here is that no RESOURCE POLICY in the supported set admits an anonymous caller, and the assessment still owes the application's own routes.

The pairing of the first two clauses is the vacuity rule in its usual costume, and here the empty response is very easy to earn: list-findings takes a REQUIRED analyzer ARN, so an account with no external-access analyzer in this Region has no ARN to pass and a stale one answers ResourceNotFoundException — either way the collection records an error rather than a finding list, which the evaluator reads as UNPROVEN. The trap is the milder cousin: a runbook that records a failed call as an empty file turns the error into a green clause, and the analyzer clauses are what catch that. The analyzer clause is therefore first, and the analyzer is per-Region — one analyzer per Region or the inventory is silently partial, and the finding count is a count for the Region it was run in. IAM roles are global, so a role trust policy that admits an external entity produces a finding in every enabled Region, which means the same defect is counted once per Region and a naive total over-reports.

There is a timing edge worth collecting beside the output rather than discovering in an assessment. Access Analyzer evaluates Block Public Access at the BUCKET level whenever a policy changes, but at the ACCOUNT level only once every six hours. Enable the account-level block and a public finding can persist for up to six hours after the access it reports has actually been blocked. Read a stale public finding against the account block settings collected in the same run before treating it as a live exposure — and never the other way round, because the reverse case, a finding that has not yet appeared, has the same six-hour window.

The account block settings are collected for their own sake and not only as context. The four booleans are the switch that decides whether a bucket CAN be made anonymous: BlockPublicAcls and IgnorePublicAcls govern the ACL path, BlockPublicPolicy and RestrictPublicBuckets the policy path, and all four are asserted because a reader who turns on two of them has closed one path and left the other open. AWS Config's own account-level rule defaults every one of the four to enforced.

Lambda function URLs deserve a sentence because they are the surface most likely to surprise. A function URL with auth type NONE performs no authentication, and it works only when the function's resource-based policy grants Principal "*" both lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and — for URLs created from October 2025 — lambda:InvokeFunction — which is a public resource policy on a supported resource type, so it surfaces here as a public finding rather than needing a call of its own. Two edges follow from AWS's own documentation: deleting a function URL does not delete that policy statement, so the finding can outlive the URL; and a NONE function URL created through the CLI or CloudFormation has no policy at all until you add one, which returns 403 to callers and produces no finding, so an absent finding is not proof that no NONE function URL exists.

API Gateway is the one anonymous surface in scope that Access Analyzer cannot see, because an HTTP API route's authorization type is not a resource policy. AWS Config's API_GWV2_AUTHORIZATION_TYPE_CONFIGURED covers it — NON_COMPLIANT when the authorization type is NONE — and it brings the ordinary Config trap with it, which is why its two companion readings are collected. A rule that was never evaluated and a rule that found nothing both return an empty EvaluationResults[], and a recorder that is not recording AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Route makes a periodic rule's silence meaningless. The rule is also REST-blind: it evaluates AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Route, so an AWS::ApiGateway::Method with authorizationType NONE on a v1 REST API is outside it and has to be read from apigateway get-method by hand.

The Cognito clause reads the field that most literally means what AC-14 says. AllowUnauthenticatedIdentities true is a pool that issues AWS credentials to a caller who presented no identity — a permitted action without identification, configured deliberately, and usually for a good reason that belongs in the security plan's rationale. The same field is asserted by the Cognito recipe for IA-08, where it carries a different claim: there it says every principal holding credentials authenticated to get them, and here it says the set of anonymous actions is empty. One field, two controls, and the duplication is deliberate — a reader arriving from either control should find it.

The vacuity to state plainly, one line per output. No analyzer means no findings and the first clause is what catches it. No identity pools means the describe call is never run, and the assertion over it returns UNPROVEN rather than PASS. An account-level public access block that has never been configured does not return four false booleans — it is the one output here whose absence is an error rather than a value, and an assessment that records no output for it has recorded nothing, not a pass.

assertions.description: An external-access analyzer is ACTIVE in the Region this collection ran in. Both external zones of trust count — an organization-scoped analyzer analyzes this account too — and naming only ACCOUNT would report a correctly configured multi-account estate as having never looked. Without this clause, an account with no analyzer and an account with nothing public are the same answer.

No external-access analyzer in this Region is stuck in CREATING, DISABLED or FAILED. An analyzer that exists and is not running is the most misleading state available: it satisfies an inventory question and analyzes nothing. The unused-access and internal-access families are deliberately outside this clause — they answer a different question and a disabled one is not an AC-14 defect.

No resource in this Region has an ACTIVE finding reporting a policy that allows public access. The claim is bounded by what an external-access analyzer reads — resource-based policies on its supported resource types — and by the six-hour lag on account-level Block Public Access evaluation, so read a finding here against the block settings collected in the same run.
New public ACLs cannot be written at the account level. One of the four switches; the ACL path is open if either of its two is false.
Public ACLs already written are ignored account-wide. Blocking new ones without ignoring the old ones leaves whatever was granted before the switch was thrown.

A bucket policy granting public access is rejected at the account level. This is the policy path's half of the same switch, and it is the one that matters for a bucket whose ACLs were never the mechanism.

Access through any public bucket policy that survives is restricted to AWS service principals and authorized users in this account. The last of the four, and the only one that constrains a policy already in place rather than the writing of one.

The identity pool named in this run does not issue AWS credentials to guests. This is AC-14's own sentence as a field: a true here is a user action performed with no identification, which the control permits only when the security plan documents the rationale. An account with no identity pools never runs the describe call and the clause returns UNPROVEN, which is correct — nothing was read.

No API Gateway v2 route has an authorization type of NONE. The rule evaluates AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Route only, so a REST API method with authorizationType NONE is outside this clause, and the rule does not exist in either AWS GovCloud (US) Region.

The configuration recorder is on. A periodic rule evaluates recorded configuration items, so a recorder that is off makes the empty NON_COMPLIANT set above indistinguishable from a route inventory nobody ever recorded.
The rule has a successful evaluation on record. A deployed-but-never-evaluated rule returns the same empty result as a compliant estate, and this is the field that separates them.

scope.note: The analyzer is per-Region and its findings are that Region's; the Config rule evaluates the recorder's inventory in the Region it is deployed to; only the S3 account-level block is account-wide. The resource types listed are the ones these commands actually read — Access Analyzer's supported set plus the route type and the account — and they are SHORTER than the estate AC-14 speaks of, which is the machine-readable half of why this recipe is partial: an anonymous route served by the reader's own application is a user action performed without authentication and appears in none of them.

recipes.evidence: Audit records read back and checked for content, rather than a setting that implies records exist. AU-03 asks what is IN a record — the type of event, when and where it occurred, its source, its outcome and the identity behind it. This recipe pulls the most recent management events out of CloudTrail and asserts that the fields carrying type, time and location are populated on the records that actually came back. It also lists the trails and the CloudWatch log groups, so the record sources this recipe does not read appear in the same output as the one it does.
recipes.expected_output: From record-sample, Events[]: one page of at most fifty of the most recent management events in the calling Region. Passing --max-results turns off the CLI's automatic pagination, so this is a sample and never the ninety-day window. Each row is the projection CloudTrail returns for a lookup: AccessKeyId, CloudTrailEvent, EventId, EventName, EventSource, EventTime, ReadOnly, Resources[] of ResourceType and ResourceName, and Username. All nine members are documented Required: No. That is the most important fact about this output, and it is why every clause below filters the rows rather than projecting a field. EventSource is the service the request was made TO. CloudTrailEvent is a JSON STRING holding the whole record body — eventVersion (1.11 at time of writing), userIdentity, eventTime, eventSource, eventName, awsRegion, sourceIPAddress, userAgent, errorCode, errorMessage, requestParameters, responseElements, requestID, eventID, eventType, eventCategory and the rest. It is not a parsed object, so no field path can reach anything inside it. The eventContext enrichment is never present in lookup-events output. The rows come from event history. AWS describes event history as a record of the past ninety days of management events in a Region, and states it is separate from any trails or event data stores. From trails, trailList[] with Name, S3BucketName, IncludeGlobalServiceEvents, IsMultiRegionTrail, HomeRegion, TrailARN and LogFileValidationEnabled, and S3KeyPrefix, SnsTopicARN, CloudWatchLogsLogGroupArn, CloudWatchLogsRoleArn, KmsKeyId, HasCustomEventSelectors, HasInsightSelectors, IsOrganizationTrail and RecursiveLogging where configured. Shadow trails — the copies of a multi-Region trail in other Regions — are returned by default. From log-groups, logGroups[] with logGroupName, creationTime, retentionInDays, metricFilterCount, arn, storedBytes, kmsKeyId, dataProtectionStatus, inheritedProperties, logGroupClass, logGroupArn and the other members the reference lists, in pages of at most fifty.
recipes.govcloud: AWS CloudTrail and Amazon CloudWatch Logs are both available in AWS GovCloud (US-West) and AWS GovCloud (US-East). Every ARN in this output uses partition arn:aws-us-gov. Three partition differences bear on what a record contains. First, CloudTrail enriched events are not supported in AWS GovCloud (US), so eventContext is absent from records in this partition; it is also absent from lookup-events output everywhere. Second, network activity events exist here only for AWS KMS, Amazon S3, AWS CloudTrail and AWS Secrets Manager, so the AwsVpceEvents eventType covers fewer sources than the commercial documentation describes. Third, since 22 November 2021, global service events from CloudFront, IAM and AWS STS are recorded in the Region where they were created, which is AWS GovCloud (US-West). A single-Region trail in AWS GovCloud (US-East) does not receive them, and AWS directs such trails to become multi-Region. That cuts against this recipe. Event history and lookup-events show those events in the Region where they occurred, so the sample can return an IAM event that no trail in the calling Region captured. The sample proves what records contain; it does not prove that a trail captured them. If you use Direct Connect, AWS directs you to enable CloudTrail in the standard AWS account rather than the AWS GovCloud (US) account. On export control: AWS states that CloudTrail logs do not contain export-controlled data and that CloudTrail configuration data may not contain it. For CloudWatch Logs, AWS lists log group names, log stream names and log group tags among the data that may leave the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and describe-log-groups returns the first and third, so neither should name anything export-controlled. The logGroupNamePattern parameter of describe-log-groups is not available in the partition; this recipe does not use it.
recipes.notes:
AU-03 names six things a record must identify: the type of event, when it occurred, where it occurred, its source, its outcome, and the identity of the subject. CloudTrail's record schema carries all six. This grammar can decide three of them from fields: type from EventName, when from EventTime, and where from EventSource, the service the request was made to. Identity is partly visible in the top-level Username, but it is not asserted, because events AWS services make on their own have no human requester. The source (sourceIPAddress, userAgent) and the outcome (errorCode, responseElements) are only inside CloudTrailEvent, which is a JSON string, so a human reads them there.

The rating is partial for three reasons. Parsing that string would fix only the last of them. (1) AU-03 covers every audit record in the system, and CloudTrail records only AWS API activity. Application logs, operating-system logs and anything the reader's own software writes have whatever content their author chose, and no clause here reads them. describe-log-groups and describe-trails are collected so those other sources are listed beside the one that was read. (2) The population is a sample of at most fifty recent events, not the record stream, so a clean result says those records were well-formed. (3) Source and outcome sit inside a string the grammar cannot address.

The record clauses do NOT depend on a trail, and this is the easiest thing to misread. AWS states that CloudTrail is enabled by default, and that event history is separate from any trails or event data stores. An account that has never created a trail still returns a full Events[], and every content clause below goes green. Those clauses therefore say nothing about whether records are being kept past ninety days, centralized, or protected from change. Those are AU-11, AU-12 and AU-09, and config-cloudtrail-audit-logging and audit-log-retention-and-delivery-failure claim them. This recipe collects describe-trails as inventory and deliberately asserts nothing over it: a trail clause here would re-prove a neighbouring control under AU-03's name.

The same fact bounds the indicator claim. KSI-MLA-OSM asks for a SIEM or similar system giving centralized, tamper-resistant logging, and FedRAMP maps AU-03 to it. This recipe serves that indicator only through record content. Event history is a single account's per-Region view, not a centralized one, even though AWS calls it immutable. Centralization and tamper resistance are proved, where they are proved at all, by the trail recipes.

Every member of the Event type is documented Required: No, EventId, EventName, EventTime and EventSource included. So each clause is a filter that selects the rows missing a field, asserted count_eq 0, and never a projection of the field across rows. A projection would drop the rows where the member is absent and report success over the rest. What the clauses assert — that the records this account actually returned carry the field — is a stronger claim than anything AWS promises.

The population clause fails only on an empty page, and an empty page means the calling Region had no management events in the last ninety days. It never means there is no trail. Read it that way before anything else.

assertions.description: The lookup returned at least one record, so the content clauses below run over a real population rather than an empty one. An empty page means the calling Region had no management events in the last ninety days. It does NOT mean no trail exists: AWS states that event history is separate from any trails, so this clause and every clause below pass on an account that has never created one.

Every record returned identifies the type of event, AU-03's first limb. Written as a filter that selects records where EventName is missing, because the member is documented Required: No. A projection over Events[].EventName would drop exactly those records and pass.
Every record returned says when the event occurred, AU-03's second limb. Same offender form, for the same reason: EventTime is Required: No, so the rows to catch are the ones missing it.

Every record returned names the service the request was made to, which is AU-03's where limb. It is not the source limb. The source of the event — the calling address and client, sourceIPAddress and userAgent — exists only inside CloudTrailEvent, and a human reads it there.

Every record returned carries the full record body. This clause proves the body arrived and deliberately claims nothing about its contents. CloudTrailEvent is a JSON string, so the source, the outcome and most of the identity inside it cannot be reached by a field path. The clause marks the line between what this recipe decides and what a human reads.

It is collected as inventory and no clause evaluates over it. describe-log-groups reads the calling Region and is also inventory.

recipes.evidence: Checks whether the continuous monitoring the reader believes is running has actually run. The question is about the programme, not one named rule. Is the recorder recording? Does any Config rule in the account fail to produce a current result? Are the standards and scanners that make up the rest of the programme in a state that yields findings? The clauses are built around one answer that looks like success and is not: a rule that has never been evaluated reports neither compliant nor non-compliant.
recipes.expected_output: From configuration-recorders, ConfigurationRecorders[] with name, roleARN, arn, and a recordingGroup of allSupported, includeGlobalResourceTypes, resourceTypes, exclusionByResourceTypes and recordingStrategy. Each also has a recordingMode whose recordingFrequency is CONTINUOUS or DAILY, and service-linked recorders carry servicePrincipal. allSupported true means Config records every supported type and picks up new types as AWS adds them. allSupported false means it records only the enumerated list, and a newly supported type is NOT recorded until somebody adds it. From configuration-recorder-status, ConfigurationRecordersStatus[] with name, recording, lastStartTime, lastStopTime, lastErrorCode, lastErrorMessage, lastStatusChangeTime, arn, and a lastStatus of Pending, Success, Failure or NotApplicable. Those lastStatus values are mixed case, unlike the upper-case enums elsewhere in this output. From config-rules, ConfigRules[] with ConfigRuleName, ConfigRuleArn, ConfigRuleId, Description, Scope, InputParameters, CreatedBy and EvaluationModes. Source.Owner is AWS, CUSTOM_LAMBDA or CUSTOM_POLICY. The optional MaximumExecutionFrequency is One_Hour, Three_Hours, Six_Hours, Twelve_Hours or TwentyFour_Hours, and a periodic rule runs every twenty-four hours by default. ConfigRuleState is ACTIVE, DELETING, DELETING_RESULTS or EVALUATING. From config-rule-evaluation-status, ConfigRulesEvaluationStatus[] with ConfigRuleName, ConfigRuleArn and ConfigRuleId, plus the invocation, evaluation, activation and error timestamps and FirstEvaluationStarted. AWS documents FirstEvaluationStarted false as meaning Config has not finished evaluating your resources against the rule at least once. Called with no rule names, the call returns status for all Config managed rules you use; the reference does not say whether custom rules are included. From config-rule-compliance, ComplianceByConfigRules[] with ConfigRuleName and a Compliance of ComplianceType plus ComplianceContributorCount (CappedCount, CapExceeded). ComplianceType is COMPLIANT, NON_COMPLIANT or INSUFFICIENT_DATA for this data type. INSUFFICIENT_DATA means no current evaluation results are available, for one of three reasons: the rule has never been invoked, its function is not delivering results, or every result was NOT_APPLICABLE because the resources were deleted or removed from the rule's scope. From security-standards, StandardsSubscriptions[] with StandardsSubscriptionArn, StandardsArn, StandardsInput, StandardsStatusReason, StandardsControlsUpdatable (READY_FOR_UPDATES or NOT_READY_FOR_UPDATES), and a StandardsStatus of PENDING, READY, INCOMPLETE, DELETING or FAILED. From guardduty-detectors, DetectorIds[]. From guardduty-detector, a Status of ENABLED or DISABLED, a FindingPublishingFrequency of FIFTEEN_MINUTES, ONE_HOUR or SIX_HOURS, ServiceRole, CreatedAt, UpdatedAt, Tags, Features, and DataSources. The API reference marks DataSources deprecated, so read Features. Status values are ENABLING, ENABLED, DISABLING, DISABLED, SUSPENDING and SUSPENDED. Accounts the call could not answer for go to failedAccounts[] instead of accounts[].
recipes.govcloud: All four services run in AWS GovCloud (US-West) and AWS GovCloud (US-East). The differences that matter here are about what the programme can cover, not whether it exists. AWS Config publishes a separate managed-rule availability list for each of the two GovCloud Regions, so a rule set built commercially will not deploy whole in the partition, and the shortfall differs between US-East and US-West. Config cannot record third-party resources or custom resource types in the partition, so allSupported means everything Config supports HERE, and SSM documents for Config remediation actions are unavailable. Security Hub CSPM does not support every control in AWS GovCloud (US), publishes its own per-Region list of unsupported controls, lacks some integrations, and aggregates across Regions only between the two GovCloud Regions. AWS states that in the China Regions and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, "it can take up to 24 hours for Security Hub CSPM to generate a preliminary security score for a standard". Separately, control findings can take up to twenty-four hours to generate or update. So a standard enabled this morning in the partition can read READY and have evaluated nothing. Amazon Inspector in AWS GovCloud (US) has neither Lambda Code Scanning nor Managed Code Repository Scanning, so resourceState.lambdaCode and resourceState.codeRepository cannot reach ENABLED there. The account-level clause below reads only state.status and is unaffected. Amazon GuardDuty in the partition lacks the entity-lists capability (IP address lists remain), lacks the IAM finding type CredentialAccess:IAMUser/CompromisedCredentials, and lacks a named set of EKS audit-log AnomalousBehavior finding types. An ENABLED detector there therefore watches for fewer things than a commercial one. AWS Config metadata must not contain export-controlled data, and AWS names rule-evaluation annotations among the fields that must not carry it.
recipes.notes:
CA-07 has two halves, and this recipe reads one of them. The operating half is telemetry: is the recorder on, do the rules evaluate, which standards are enabled, do the scanners cover the account. The clauses below decide that half. The half the control actually names is a strategy: which metrics were chosen, how often they are checked, who correlates the results and who reports them. No call returns that document, and the telemetry is what the document is measured against, not a substitute for it. Hence partial.

The vacuity this recipe closes is not the usual empty list. describe-compliance-by-config-rule returns INSUFFICIENT_DATA, not NON_COMPLIANT, for a rule that has never run. So the obvious clause, "no rule is NON_COMPLIANT", is TRUE on an estate where no rule has ever been evaluated. Two clauses below close the gap. One asserts FirstEvaluationStarted is true on every rule the evaluation-status call returns, which catches a rule that has never completed an evaluation. The other asserts no rule reports INSUFFICIENT_DATA, which also catches a rule that has stopped producing results. That second clause fails in one healthy case: a rule whose resources were all deleted or moved out of its scope. A FAIL there needs a human to decide which of AWS's three documented causes applies, and the clause is kept anyway, because without it the compliance output passes on an idle estate.

Other recipes here assert FirstEvaluationStarted for the rules they name. This one is unfiltered, so it claims something about the whole set the call returns. That set is documented as all Config managed rules you use. The reference does not say whether CUSTOM_LAMBDA and CUSTOM_POLICY rules are included, so the claim is made for managed rules. A custom rule absent from the response is outside the clause, not proved live.

recordingGroup.allSupported is collected but deliberately not asserted. A recorder with allSupported false and an explicit resourceTypes list is a legitimate design, not a defect, and turning it into a FAIL would be an architectural judgement this site has no standing to make. What deserves a human's attention is the consequence AWS documents: with allSupported false, a newly supported resource type is not recorded until somebody adds it, so the recording group ages. Read exclusionByResourceTypes beside it.

The indicator claim needs one qualification stated plainly. KSI-MLA-EVC asks that the configuration of machine-based information resources — "especially infrastructure as code" — be persistently evaluated and tested. This recipe evaluates DEPLOYED configuration only. Nothing here reads a template, a plan or a policy-as-code result before deployment, and that half of the indicator belongs to the pipeline plane. The Config and Security Hub clauses serve the indicator. The GuardDuty and Inspector clauses name only ca-7: GuardDuty evaluates behaviour and Inspector evaluates software vulnerabilities, and neither reads configuration. They are here because CA-07's monitoring programme is broader than its configuration half.

StandardsStatus READY means Security Hub can run checks and calculate a score. It does not mean it has. AWS documents up to twenty-four hours to generate or update control findings, and up to twenty-four hours for the preliminary score in AWS GovCloud (US). On the Config side, the INSUFFICIENT_DATA clause catches an enabled programme with no evaluations. Security Hub has no equivalent clause here, and this recipe does not pretend otherwise.

lastStatus is asserted against Failure, not for Success, on purpose. The documented values are Pending, Success, Failure and NotApplicable, and a recorder that has just started legitimately reports Pending. A clause demanding Success would fail a healthy estate. Failure is the only value that is unambiguously wrong.

Inspector's account-level state is what the clause reads. resourceState carries a separate status for each scan type, and the reference does not say whether an account can be ENABLED while its EC2 or ECR scanning is not. A human should read resourceState before treating an account-level PASS as coverage of a particular resource type.

Every call here is Regional. A programme that is complete in one Region and absent in another returns a clean result from whichever Region you called. That is the largest gap between what this recipe proves and what CA-07 asks.

assertions.description: The configuration recorder is on. This is the population clause for everything Config-based below: rules cannot evaluate resources whose configuration is not recorded, so a FAIL here makes the rule clauses meaningless, not merely red. An account with no recorder returns an empty list, and this clause comes back UNPROVEN.

No recorder's most recent recording event failed. Asserted against Failure rather than for Success because a recorder that has just started legitimately reports Pending, and demanding Success would fail a healthy estate. The value is mixed case as documented.

At least one Config rule is active. This is the population clause for the two evaluation clauses below, which are count_eq 0 and would otherwise pass on an account with no rules. The pipe matters: without it, [0] indexes each matched object instead of the filtered list.

Every rule the evaluation-status call returns has completed at least one evaluation. AWS documents FirstEvaluationStarted false as meaning Config has not finished evaluating your resources against the rule at least once. Comparing against the JSON literal true catches false rows and rows where the field is missing. Called with no names, the call is documented to return all Config managed rules you use, so the claim covers managed rules. Whether custom rules appear is not stated.

No rule reports that no current evaluation results are available. Without this clause, 'no rule is NON_COMPLIANT' is true on an estate where nothing has run, because AWS returns INSUFFICIENT_DATA, not NON_COMPLIANT, in that case. AWS documents three causes: the rule was never invoked, its function is not delivering results, or every result was NOT_APPLICABLE because the resources were deleted or removed from its scope. The third can occur on a healthy estate. A FAIL is a prompt for a human to decide which cause applies, not a finding in itself.

At least one Security Hub standard is subscribed. This is the population clause for the status clause below, and the only evidence in this recipe that the estate is measured against a published benchmark rather than only against rules somebody chose.

Every subscribed standard finished enabling. PENDING means Security Hub is still adding controls, and INCOMPLETE means it could not enable the standard completely. Both describe a standard that is attached and not fully measuring. READY means Security Hub runs checks for every applicable enabled control, but it describes the subscription, not results. AWS documents up to twenty-four hours to generate or update control findings, and up to twenty-four hours for a preliminary score in AWS GovCloud (US).

The detector the reader named is enabled. A detector can exist in a DISABLED state, and list-detectors still returns its id while nothing is analysed, which is why this clause reads the status rather than the id. It serves CA-07's monitoring breadth and deliberately not KSI-MLA-EVC, because GuardDuty evaluates behaviour, not configuration.

The Inspector status call returned at least one account. This is the population clause for the state clause below, which is count_eq 0 and would otherwise pass on an empty accounts[]. That happens when the call answers for nobody, because accounts it cannot answer for go to failedAccounts[] instead.

No account came back in failedAccounts[]. An account Inspector could not answer for is missing from accounts[], not present and failing, so the state clause cannot see it. Written as not_exists on the first entry, so the clause passes whether an empty failedAccounts is returned as [] or omitted.

No account in accounts[] has an Inspector state other than ENABLED. The documented values include ENABLING and SUSPENDING, which are transitional, and DISABLED and SUSPENDED, which are not. All four fail here; re-run before acting on the transitional two. This reads the account-level state only. resourceState carries a separate status for each scan type, and a human should read it before treating a PASS as coverage of EC2 or ECR.

scope.note: All nine calls are Regional, and none widens the set. Config, Security Hub, GuardDuty and Inspector each answer for the Region the call was made in, so a monitoring programme that is complete in us-east-1 and absent in us-west-2 returns a clean result from the first. Two calls are narrower still. get-detector names one detector id. batch-get-account-status without --account-ids answers only for the calling account. Neither reads an organization. describe-config-rule-evaluation-status called with no names is documented to cover the Config managed rules in use; whether custom rules appear is not stated, so they may fall outside the evaluation clause's population.

recipes.expected_output: Under get-account-summary, four integers: AccountMFAEnabled is 1 when the root user has an MFA device and 0 otherwise, Users sizes the IAM user population, and MFADevices and MFADevicesInUse size the authenticator estate. Under list-virtual-mfa-devices, one row per ASSIGNED virtual (TOTP app) device — SerialNumber is the device ARN, which for a virtual device always has the form arn:<partition>:iam::<account>:mfa/<name>, and UserArn is the principal it is assigned to; a root device shows UserArn ending in :root. The list is the set of principals who can currently sign in by typing a code from an app, whatever other devices they also hold. Under privileged-group-members, the IAM users in the named group, which is the reader's own statement of the privileged population. credential-report is the CSV described on the iam-credential-report recipe, one row per IAM user plus <root_account>, with password_enabled and mfa_active as TRUE/FALSE strings. Under list-instances, zero or one Identity Center instance.
recipes.govcloud: IAM and IAM Identity Center are available in both AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and every call here runs unchanged; ARNs use partition arn:aws-us-gov, so a virtual device's SerialNumber reads arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<account>:mfa/<name>. The root user is different in the partition, and the two root assertions must be read with that in mind: AWS documents that a GovCloud account's root user cannot sign in to the console — initial access is an Administrator IAM user or the OrganizationAccountAccessRole — and that the supported MFA devices cannot be attached to that root user, so AccountMFAEnabled will be 0 there and the eq 1 assertion FAILS on every GovCloud account by construction. Read that failure as not applicable, evidence the root user's credential instead from AccountAccessKeysPresent on the identity-sources-and-root-credential-lockdown recipe, and apply the phishing-resistance question to the Administrator user, who is an ordinary IAM user in this output. AWS also documents that GovCloud users can use the same FIDO security keys and virtual authenticator apps as commercial users but need a partition-specific hardware TOTP token, and that an Identity Center instance in the partition is reached over FIPS endpoints with no multi-Region support.
recipes.notes:
IA-02 (01) and (02) each ask for multi-factor authentication for a population, and FedRAMP's guidance on both is that the factor be phishing-resistant. AWS names which of its factors are: its IAM MFA page says FIDO-based passkeys and security keys are resistant to phishing, man-in-the-middle and replay attacks and provide a stronger level of security than TOTP-based options. The measurable half of both enhancements is therefore not whether MFA is on — the credential report and the Config rules already settle that under IA-02 base — but which factor a principal holds, and the only factor an API names by shape is the virtual one: ListVirtualMFADevices returns every assigned TOTP-app device with the principal it belongs to, and MFADevice documents that a virtual device's serial number is the device ARN. A principal on that list can be phished through that device regardless of what else they have registered (a user may hold up to eight), which is why the list is read as the offender population rather than joined against ListMFADevices per user. What no API distinguishes is a hardware TOTP token from a security key — both are non-virtual and only one is phishing-resistant — so a principal absent from the virtual list is a principal whose factor a human confirms by eye or from the device inventory.

The partition between the two enhancements is the reader's, not AWS's: nothing in IAM marks a user privileged. This recipe takes the reader's designation as a group name and lists its members, so the (01) reading is the intersection of privileged-group-members with list-virtual-mfa-devices, plus the root user, which is privileged by definition and is the one principal the assertions can decide alone. The (02) reading is the complement — every row of the credential report not in the group — and it is left to the reader because the assertion grammar cannot subtract one output from another. Both readings assume IAM users are a sign-in population at all: on an estate whose workforce arrives through IAM Identity Center or an external IdP, Users may be 0 and the whole question moves to the identity source, whose MFA mode and permitted types — authenticator apps, security keys and built-in authenticators — are chosen in the Identity Center console and are exposed by no sso-admin operation, and which an external IdP enforces where the estate never sees it. list-instances is here so the reader knows that path exists.

IA-02 (08) asks that the mechanism be replay-resistant, which is a different property from the phishing resistance the two enhancements above turn on, and the two must not be read with one list. NIST SP 800-63B §5.2.8 defines the property and names the authenticators that have it: OTP devices, cryptographic authenticators and look-up secrets are replay-resistant, and memorized secrets are not, because the secret itself is what is presented each time. So a TOTP app fails (01) and (02) — AWS ranks it below FIDO precisely because it can be phished — and still satisfies (08), and the offender population for (08) is the one IAM shape NIST excludes: a password with no second factor. Access keys are outside that population too, because SigV4 signs every request with a time stamp AWS enforces — a request must reach AWS within five minutes of it or is denied — and a FIDO assertion is a signed answer to a fresh challenge, which is what AWS's own replay-attack sentence names. A principal with password_enabled TRUE and mfa_active FALSE authenticates with a memorized secret alone, so the offender count for (08) is that row set, evaluated over the credential report's IAM users and root. Whether the console session that follows a federated sign-in is replay-resistant is a property of the SAML or OIDC exchange with the IdP and is not read here.

generate-credential-report is asynchronous and a stored report is served for up to four hours; run it, then read. Substitute <PRIVILEGED_GROUP_NAME> with the group you would name in the SSP as holding privileged access; an account that partitions privilege by policy attachment rather than group membership should read the AC-06 recipes for the population and use this output for the factor.

assertions.description: The root user — the account's most privileged principal, and the one nothing else partitions — has an MFA device. In AWS GovCloud (US) this is 0 by construction; see the GovCloud note.

No virtual (TOTP app) device is assigned to the root user. With the flag above this leaves a passkey, a security key or a hardware TOTP token; only the first two are phishing-resistant, and which one it is comes from the device itself, not from any API.

No IAM principal, root included, can authenticate with a password alone — the one authenticator NIST SP 800-63B §5.2.8 says is not replay-resistant. OTP devices and cryptographic authenticators are, by the same section, and signed API requests carry a five-minute timestamp window, so the offender population is exactly the password-only rows. This is replay resistance, not phishing resistance: a TOTP app passes here and fails IA-02 (01)/(02).

scope.note: The IAM calls are global and answer once and completely for this account, and the credential report is per account with no organization-wide equivalent. `sso-admin list-instances` is the narrow call: it returns the instance only in its home Region, so an empty list is as consistent with the wrong Region as with no Identity Center at all. `privileged-group-members` has the reader's group as its population — a privileged user who is not in that group is invisible to the (01) reading, and the assertions do not read that output at all.

recipes.notes:
IA-05 (01) has eight limbs and this output decides one of them for one population. Limb (h) — the composition and complexity rules the organization defined — is what an IAM account password policy is, and the recipe reads it twice: GetAccountPasswordPolicy states the rules the account enforces, and the IAM_PASSWORD_POLICY rule compares them with the values the deploying team wrote into its parameters, which is where the organization-defined numbers live. The parameters row is collected for that reason: an empty NON_COMPLIANT set from a rule deployed with no parameters proves only that some custom policy exists, and the third assertion checks that at least the length value was written down. The number itself is the reader's — FedRAMP's dataset carries no parameter value for this enhancement, so no assertion here compares length or age against a figure.

The other limbs are either decided by the identity source's contract or by nothing here. Limbs (a) and (b), the list of commonly used, expected or compromised passwords: IAM has no such check and offers no setting for one; IAM Identity Center documents that passwords publicly known through a data set leaked from a third party cannot be used, which satisfies both limbs for users created in its directory by contract, with no setting to read and no frequency to verify. Limb (c), transmission over cryptographically protected channels, is TLS on every AWS sign-in endpoint by contract. Limb (d), salted key-derivation storage, is inside AWS and is read from AWS's own authorization package via AWS Artifact, not from any call. Limbs (e), (f) and (g) — a new password on recovery, long passphrases with spaces and all printable characters, and tooling that helps a user choose — are properties of the sign-in and reset interfaces that no output here observes; IAM permits up to 128 characters and Identity Center 8 to 64, and neither page states whether a space is accepted.

The population is the judgement that decides whether any of this matters. get-account-summary's Users is the size of the IAM password population; an estate whose workforce signs in through Identity Center or an external IdP may show 0, in which case the IAM policy governs nobody and the whole enhancement moves to the identity source — Identity Center's fixed rules (8 to 64 characters, one character from each of four classes, no reuse of the last three, the leaked-password check) for its own directory, or the external IdP's policy for a federated one, and which of those the instance uses is read in the Identity Center console, not from list-instances. Deploy the periodic Config rule in exactly one Region: it evaluates a global resource and adding it elsewhere adds evaluations rather than coverage.

assertions.description: A custom account password policy is set. The CLI returns a NoSuchEntity error rather than a document when only the AWS default applies, so this reads UNPROVEN in that case and the Config rule below is what turns the default into a recorded failure.
The account policy meets every parameter the rule was deployed with, and the rule is NON_COMPLIANT by its own definition when the default policy is in use.

The rule was deployed with a minimum-length value, so the empty NON_COMPLIANT set above means the policy meets the organization's number rather than merely existing. A rule with no InputParameters reads UNPROVEN here.

The customer-managed configuration recorder is on — with no recorder the list is empty and this is UNPROVEN, and with a stopped one an empty NON_COMPLIANT set is indistinguishable from a clean estate.
iam-password-policy has evaluated at least once; a deployed-but-never-evaluated rule also returns an empty result, and a rule that is not deployed makes the call fail rather than return nothing.
The rule has a successful evaluation on record.

scope.note: The account password policy is one object per account and global; get-account-password-policy and get-account-summary answer completely for this account. The Config rule evaluates in the calling Region and is deliberately deployed in one, and `sso-admin list-instances` returns the instance only in its home Region — that is the narrow call, and an empty list there does not mean IAM users are the only password population.
